conceptTag: Google wasn't the first search engine
readerTitle: Google was late to search. Why didn't that matter?
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Google, AltaVista, Yahoo, Excite, Lycos, GoTo.com/Overture) + 가상 적용 (물류 센서 제조사)
insight: 먼저 들어갔는지가 아니라, 먼저 들어가서 고객을 붙잡아 둘 무언가(전환 비용, 네트워크, 희소 자원)가 생겼는지를 본다.
misconception: 시장에 먼저 들어간 회사가 이긴다. 이미 강자가 있는 시장에는 늦었다.

sources.text: Brin, S. & Page, L. (1998). The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine. Stanford University (PageRank 설명)
Google, company history ('Our story'): 1998년 9월 법인 설립, Stanford 연구 프로젝트에서 시작
Yahoo! and Google press release (June 2000): Google이 Yahoo 검색 결과를 제공하기로 한 계약
GoTo.com/Overture 역사 자료 및 언론 보도: 1998년 입찰 방식 검색 광고 도입
United States v. Google LLC, U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, memorandum opinion (August 2024)
Lieberman, M. & Montgomery, D. (1988). First-Mover Advantages. Strategic Management Journal.

factChecks.note: 초기 검색엔진 출시 연도: WebCrawler·Lycos·Yahoo 1994년, AltaVista·Excite 1995년(Excite의 전신 Architext는 1993년). 카드에는 "1994 and 1995"로만 적었습니다. 게시 전 각 회사 연혁으로 다시 확인하세요.
1990년대 후반 경쟁사들이 뉴스·이메일·날씨 등을 붙인 '포털' 전략으로 간 것은 널리 기록된 내용이지만, 회사별 시점은 다릅니다. 카드에는 일반적으로만 적었습니다.
Yahoo가 2000년 6월 Google을 검색 결과 제공사로 선택한 계약은 양사 보도자료로 확인하세요. 시장 점유율 수치는 확실하지 않아 넣지 않았습니다.
GoTo.com(이후 Overture)의 입찰식 검색 광고는 1998년 시작. Google AdWords는 2000년 출시, 클릭당 과금과 광고 품질(클릭률) 반영은 2002년경 도입. 카드에는 "later", "also weighed how often people clicked"로만 적었습니다.
2024년 8월 미국 연방지방법원 판결: Google이 브라우저·휴대폰 제조사와의 기본 검색엔진 계약 등을 통해 검색 독점을 불법 유지했다고 판단. 항소·구제 조치 진행 상황을 게시 직전에 확인하세요.
"1998년에는 앞으로 인터넷을 쓸 사람 대부분이 아직 온라인이 아니었다"는 정성적 표현입니다. 구체적 수치는 넣지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Google wasn't the first search engine.
body: WebCrawler, Lycos, Yahoo, AltaVista and Excite all launched in 1994 and 1995. Millions of people already used them.
Google was incorporated in September 1998, years behind. It went on to beat every one of them. Being first, it turns out, wasn't worth much here.

image.label: Old search boxes lined up, with a late plain one at the end
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 1990년대 풍 브라우저 창 다섯 개가 출발선에 줄지어 있고, 맨 끝에 늦게 도착한 아주 단순한 검색창 하나. 실제 회사 로고나 이름은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: It's 1998. You have a better way to rank results.
body: Several search engines are already well known and well funded. Their results are often cluttered or off-target. You and a co-founder have a method that ranks pages better.
What's your best move?

options.text: Don't launch. The early players already own search
options.feedback: You avoid a costly fight, but you assume their head start is locked in. Ask first what actually stops their users from leaving.

options.text: Launch a plain search page and compete only on better results
options.feedback: Searchers can switch by typing a new address, so quality can win. The cost: you skip the extras that rivals use to hold attention.

options.text: Launch a full portal with news and email to match the leaders
options.feedback: You'd look like a serious rival. But you'd spread a small team thin and copy the leaders' weakest area: the search itself.

cards.title: The leaders drifted. Google stayed on one job.
body: In the late 1990s, many search companies turned into portals, adding news, email, weather and shopping to keep visitors on their pages.
Google kept a nearly empty homepage. Its edge was **PageRank**: it ranked a page higher when many other pages linked to it, especially important ones.
Results got noticeably better. In 2000, Yahoo chose Google to power its own search results.

image.label: A crowded portal page beside a single search box
image.brief: 좌우 비교 일러스트. 왼쪽은 뉴스·날씨·쇼핑 배너로 꽉 찬 웹페이지, 오른쪽은 흰 바탕에 검색창 하나뿐인 페이지. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Being first only helps if something locks customers in.
body: **First-mover advantage** is real only when the early lead turns into something that stays. Common locks:
list: **Switching costs:** leaving takes money, time or retraining
**Network effects:** each user makes it better for the others
**Scarce assets:** the best locations, suppliers or licenses
**Learning that stays hidden:** know-how rivals can't copy
cards.callout: Early search had almost none of these. Switching took one new web address.

cards.title: The late mover got three gifts.
body: **Free lessons.** The pioneers had shown what people searched for and what annoyed them.
**Better conditions.** The web had grown, so there were far more links to learn from. Link-based ranking works better on a bigger web.
**A market still ahead.** In 1998, most people who would ever search online weren't online yet. The leaders had a head start, not the whole market.

cards.title: Google was late to search ads too.
body: In 1998, GoTo.com (later Overture) began selling search ads ranked by how much advertisers bid.
Google's ad system came later. It also weighed how often people clicked on an ad, so useful ads could beat high bids.
Again, the first idea came from someone else. The better version, built when the market was still growing, took the prize.

cards.title: Late isn't a strategy on its own.
body: Many latecomers to search vanished. Google won with a clearly better product, not by waiting. Stories like this one hide the failures.

And once Google led, it built its own locks, including deals to be the default search engine in browsers and phones. In 2024, a US court ruled that Google used such deals to illegally keep its monopoly.
Leads without locks are rented. Leaders know it.

cards.title: Now you make sensors for warehouses.
body: You've built a better pallet-tracking sensor. Two rivals got there first.
Rival X sells tags that work with any scanner, bought month to month. Rival Y's tags run on a warehouse system customers spent months installing and training staff on. Which lead is harder to attack?

options.text: Rival X. It has sold to more warehouses for longer
options.feedback: More customers looks strong, but they can switch next month. Time in market isn't a lock.

options.text: Rival Y. Switching means redoing installation and training
options.feedback: Y's head start became a switching cost. Attack X first, or make moving from Y cheap, for example by doing the setup for free.

options.text: Neither. A better sensor will beat both
options.feedback: True against X, where quality alone can win. Against Y, a better sensor still asks customers to pay the cost of switching.

cards.softwareNote: The same test applies to apps. A tool people can swap in a minute has a thin lead. A tool holding a team's data, workflows and integrations has a thick one.

cards.title: Don't ask who was first. Ask what being first locked in.
body: If nothing keeps customers from leaving, an early lead can be overtaken by a better product.
**Try it today:** pick your strongest rival. List what would stop one of their customers from switching to you tomorrow. If the list is short, their lead is smaller than it looks.
cards.next: Next · Launch now or wait? You make the call.
